21.0.0.en: Nob: located northeast of Jerusalem and 8 km from Gibeah, the town of Saul. It was counted as a city of the priests because the tabernacle of meeting was moved to it after the destruction of Shiloh, although it was not among the priestly cities that Joshua assigned (Josh 21). The First Book of Samuel. The town of "Nob" was the town to which the tabernacle of meeting was moved after it had been for a time in the town of "Shiloh", and consequently the high priest "Ahimelech the son of Ahitub", the son of "Eli", also moved to it; he was the same as "Ahijah the son of Ahitub" or his brother (1 Sam 14:3, 18), and "Abiathar" the priest, his son, helped him in the service (1 Chr 15:11, Mk 2:26). When Ahimelech saw David he was amazed and afraid at his unexpected visit, and because he was alone and without a retinue of men, as ought to have been the case since he was a military commander, and he asked him the reason for his sudden visit and his coming alone ...

21.0.1.en: When the Book of Chronicles or the Gospel of Mark mentions that David met Abiathar the high priest at Nob, what is meant is that he was the son of Ahimelech, for he was with him and would become high priest after him. Christ did not say that Abiathar was the one who gave David the bread, but said "in the days of Abiathar."

21.0.2.en: David's coming to Nob was to ask for the prayers of Ahimelech and his son Abiathar, in addition to asking them for food and a weapon, as will appear in the following verses.

21.1.0.en: David answered Ahimelech with a lie, for he feared to inform him of Saul's pursuit of him and his seeking to kill him (and of course this was a point of human weakness into which David ought not to have fallen, but God shows us pictures of human weakness so that we also may learn from them). David told him that he was sent by the king on a secret mission that he could not disclose, as the king's command, and he answered him about the young men that he had appointed for them places to hide here and there. God forgave David his lie and his not turning to Him in prayer or asking Samuel, because he always returns to Him quickly in repentance and does not persist in his sins like Saul, for indeed his heart is like the heart of God.

21.2.0.en: What is there under your hand?! With this question David expressed his need for food, and then asked Ahimelech for five loaves for himself and the young men, or anything available and at hand to eat.

21.3.0.en: Common bread: that is, ordinary bread that it is lawful for any person to eat.

21.3.1.en: Holy bread: what is meant is the showbread of the table of the presence, which none but the priests eat.

21.3.2.en: Ahimelech answered David that he had no ready bread that the men could eat, but the bread available and present at the moment was the showbread, which none but the priests eat. But as a kind of flexibility, to save the situation and to make David's and the king's mission succeed, "Ahimelech" indicated that David could take the bread and eat it with the young men if they were physically clean and had not touched their wives.

21.4.0.en: Today also it will be sanctified in the vessel: the new bread placed in the vessel on the table of the showbread is sanctified by being placed in it; that is, after my taking the common bread, holy bread remains in the tabernacle of meeting. Common in a way: the bread had been taken off the table, and therefore in a case of great need such as David's it was possible for them to eat it, lest he and his men faint on the way, on condition of their cleanness.

21.4.1.en: David assured Ahimelech the priest that he and his men were clean and had not touched women for two days, since they left "Gibeah of Saul", and that the young men's vessels also were clean, untouched by anything unclean, and therefore the matter became lawful, with no evil in it.

21.5.0.en: After "David" had reassured "Ahimelech" the priest, he took the bread from him, which was the old bread that the priest had taken off the table and replaced with new bread.

21.5.1.en: Among the beautiful things David did was that the first place he decided to take refuge in was the house of the Lord and the first person he spoke with was the priest. Perhaps we too should do this, so that the Church is the first place we turn to, for God's blessing in His house is what supports you in all the steps of your life, gives you favor in the eyes of all whom you meet and guides you to good conduct.

21.6.0.en: This verse mentions a man who would have a role in the later events (ch. 22). This man worked for Saul as chief of his herdsmen, and it happened that he was present in the tabernacle of meeting, since a vow was upon him or a necessity called him to be there, which is what the inspired text expressed by the phrase "detained." We know from his name that his origin was Edomite, that is, of the offspring of Esau, and he had become a Jew, so he was one of Saul's followers. The First Book of Samuel

21.7.0.en: "David" hastened to make a second request of Ahimelech the priest, which was that he supply him with any weapon, and he gave his excuse for not carrying his weapon, namely his haste in leaving according to the king's command, which made him forget his weapon.

21.8.0.en: Ahimelech answered David that he had no weapon except the sword of Goliath the Philistine whom he had killed before. The people had kept this sword in the tabernacle of meeting as a memorial of God's work with them, and Ahimelech had hidden it in a corner of the tent and placed before it the "ephod", which is one of the priests' garments and has been spoken of often before. David took the sword and said that there was none like it, for two reasons:

21.8.1.en: 1- Because it was well made, since this mighty man Goliath used it.

21.8.2.en: 2- Because it reminds him of God's work and His protection of him from Goliath, so he always remembers God's support of him when he has this sword with him.

21.8.3.en: We note that when David killed Goliath, which was the greatest offering a person could offer to God at that time because it was in place of his life, God blessed him and afterward gave him the sword of Goliath to fight with, and preserved him in all of Saul's pursuits of him. So when a person gives something to God, God blesses him and gives him more and more.

21.9.s.en: (2) David's flight to "Gath" and his feigning madness

21.9.0.en: We have already pointed out that "Gath" is one of the five great cities of the Philistines, and its king was Achish. "David" went to it in an unexpected step, but he went to it as a political refugee, to use the expression we use now. David's thinking was that Gath was the place where Saul would not search or attack that great city for the sake of David. It was an unusual courage on David's part to flee to Gath, because he was exposed to death there, but he may have said to himself that Achish would receive him out of spite toward Saul, because he was an enemy of Saul, and if he saw that David had left Saul and joined him, he would gain a hero with whom to fight Saul; yet fear remained within him that Achish might arrest him and kill him.

21.10.0.en: We understand from the text that Achish accepted David to take refuge in his city, or at least paid no attention to his presence, but the leaders of his people and his counselors did not like that, so they spoke to Achish, reminding him that David was the man who had brought shame upon the Philistines by killing Goliath, and that he was the hero of Israel for whom the women chanted.

21.11.0.en: These words reached "David", and he feared greatly that "Achish" would be influenced by his aides and their words and would kill him, and therefore he came up with a new idea, which was to feign madness and insanity. He began to let his spittle run down his beard and to scratch with his nails on the doors like madmen.

21.11.1.en: We note that to save his life David resorted to human means and did not turn to God, who is able to save him from evil. He began first by lying to the priest, then taking refuge in the cities of the enemies without seeking God's opinion, and with his human thinking he also pretended madness to save his life, forgetting what he had said earlier to Goliath, that his strength was in the name of the Lord of hosts!! ... My beloved brother, do not resort to lying at times of danger or pressure on you, but turn to God and leave the arrangement to Him. Stand firm in your faith even if thought fights you that matters will become complicated, for God is able to solve all your problems if you trust in Him.

21.12.0.en: The purpose of the men in speaking with "Achish" was to bring David to him so that he would try him and pass the sentence of death on him, but here we see God's work to protect "David", for He put it in the heart of "Achish" that David had become a madman, so how could he bring him into his council or into his house; he rebuked this conduct in himself before his men and indeed refused to do anything with David.

21.12.1.en: David was praying in all these situations, and he prayed Psalm "34"; for this reason God saved him despite his human weakness in lying, because he was a righteous man and wronged, and God defends His weak children who take refuge in Him.

21.12.2.en: The men rally around David and Saul kills the priests

22.0.s.en: (1) David goes to Adullam and then to Mizpeh of Moab

22.0.0.en: David left Nob and Gath and headed to his own country, Adullam, located 12 miles southwest of Bethlehem in the land of Judah. When his brothers and all his father's relatives heard, they went to him, and with them also went all the men who were distressed by Saul or who were suffering financial hardship and could not pay. The number of those gathered around him was about 400 men, whose motives differed: his family feared Saul, who might take revenge on them out of spite toward David, while the rest of the men were driven by distress to follow David, since they saw in him a deliverer from Saul's injustice and their hard circumstances, especially as poverty had increased among the children of Israel because of the repeated attacks of the Philistines and their plundering of the people. By David's competence as a leader he was able to turn them into a fighting army that he led himself. We see here the benefit of the Philistines' uprising against David in Gath, that he was compelled to leave it and return to his country and be subject to God and under His protection, and God blessed him with the rallying of 400 men around him, so that he became a great force; and at Adullam he chanted Psalm (57). David here is a type of Christ, for the weary and distressed gathered around him as sinners and tax collectors came to Christ, and He took away their sins and they became a great army, which is the flock of Christ that enters the Kingdom. As for Saul, who reigned with apparent power over the kingdom, he is a type of Satan, who reigns over the world, but his end is destruction, as Saul was killed in the battle with the Philistines (ch. 31).

22.1.0.en: David continued his flight with his men and his family. He left the land of Judah and crossed the Jordan to its east, where the land of the Moabites is, and met their king in his town "Mizpeh of Moab" and asked him to let his father and mother stay in this town to protect them from Saul's violence, until he could work out his affairs and know what God wanted for him in the coming days; and indeed he left them as guests of the king of Moab, while he hid in one of the fortified places in the lands of the Moabites. David took refuge in Moab because one of his grandmothers, Ruth, was a Moabite (Ruth 4:17), so there was a bond of kinship between him and Moab. In addition there was enmity between Saul and Moab, since Saul had fought them and defeated them (ch. 14:47).

22.2.0.en: Gad the prophet: mentioned in the incident of the numbering of the people (2 Sam 24:11-15) and in (2 Chr 29:

22.2.1.en: 25) in the arrangement of the musical service. Some think that he was one of the disciples of Samuel the prophet in the school of the prophets, and that Samuel charged Gad to follow David because he knew that he was the man of God and the true king. God visited "David" through one of His prophets, "Gad the prophet" or the seer, as the prophets used to be called anciently, and "Gad" informed David that he must leave the stronghold, which was one of the strongholds of Moab, and return to the land of Judah. David obeyed the message and came to a place in the land of Judah called "the forest of Hereth", a wooded region southwest of Bethlehem.

22.2.2.en: Listen to the voice of God even if it is contrary to what you are thinking, for God arranges all things for the salvation of your soul, and accept God's guidance in humility. David was a prophet, yet he accepted the guidance of Gad the prophet, and in this God leads you and protects you and no one can harm you.

22.3.0.en: The fame of David and his men spread, since their number was large and noticeable, and the matter reached Saul the king, who gathered with his men and servants in his town Gibeah, and under the shade of the tamarisk tree he addressed them, filled with wrath and envy. He said to them, You are of the tribe of Benjamin and of the sons of my clan, and it is I who gave you vineyards and fields and made you captains of thousands over all the people and captains of hundreds, so has David the son of Jesse given you anything in return?! Of course Saul's words to his men were meant to win them to himself and to incite them against David, that he was poor, and that even if he became king Saul and his men expected that he would honor the men of his tribe of Judah and not the men of Benjamin.

22.3.1.en: Saul's weakness appears from this, because he relied on himself in pride and not on God, so he went seeking support from his tribe against David. As for Moses, who relied on God, his disciple Joshua was from the tribe of Ephraim while Moses was from the tribe of Levi, and Moses did not set up his sons as leaders. And David also, when he became king, had a wide heart, and received Abner the commander of Saul's army, and Amasa and others ...

22.4.0.en: You have conspired against me: you have plotted against me.

22.4.1.en: Saul continues his speech in order to win the sympathy of his men, saying to them, Why then did you not rally around me, and why have you plotted against me, and I find no one who pities me or sympathizes with me, when my son (Jonathan) has gone and allied himself with my enemy "David", and they have set up a plan against me to kill me and an ambush for my destruction, and none of you told me of the agreement made between them. Of course Saul's words were a lie by which he wanted to incite the men against David in order to kill him, and to arouse pity for himself over the alleged plot. All this confirms Saul's weakness, for since he had departed from God he went on stirring people up against David and feeling that he was wronged and neglected by his clan, and the truth is that his heart was empty of God, and therefore he suffered from smallness of soul.

22.5.0.en: Doeg the Edomite was the man who was in the tabernacle of meeting when "David" met "Ahimelech" the priest (ch. 21:7), and he was the one who began to answer Saul here in order to declare his allegiance to him and his hostility to David. He began to relate to him the details of David's meeting with Ahimelech and how Ahimelech gave David bread and also the sword of Goliath, and he added that Ahimelech inquired of the Lord for him, in order to show Ahimelech's sympathy with David and to stir up Saul against Ahimelech. Doeg and his work and lineage were spoken of before in (ch. 21).

22.5.1.en: Do not seize opportunities to win the love of others by condemnation and by stirring people up against one another, for in this you are an agent of Satan, spreading evil and disputes among people and challenging God, so you lose His mercy and divine punishment awaits you.

22.6.s.en: (3) Saul kills the priests of the Lord

22.6.0.en: After the denunciation of "Doeg", Saul was very greatly enraged, so he sent his servants with a message to bring Ahimelech the priest and all the priests with him from "Nob", the city of the priests and the tabernacle of meeting at that time. When they came before Saul, Saul began to speak in a manner that showed contempt for Ahimelech, for he did not mention his name but called him by his father's name, in a tone of wrath and threat of evil, and Ahimelech answered him in humility, "Here I am, my lord."

22.7.0.en: Saul spoke directly to Ahimelech and the priests, charging them with conspiracy and with helping David against the king by giving him bread and the sword and praying for him to remain hidden and lying in wait for the king. Of course Ahimelech meant no evil against the king when he helped David, for David was fleeing from the king and not lurking for him or wanting to do the king any harm.

22.8.0.en: Ahimelech began to speak in his own defense in a logical and sober manner, and we can summarize his defense in two main points:

22.8.1.en: A- The character of David: he described him as a valiant man of courage with none like him among the people, and also as the king's son-in-law, his confidant, who always has a place at the king's table, that is, a person far removed from any suspicion.

22.8.2.en: B- His lack of knowledge: this is Ahimelech's second defense, that he knew nothing of the quarrel between David and Saul, or David's flight, or David's conspiring against the king.

22.8.3.en: In all this Ahimelech was telling the truth, and he asked Saul not to charge him or his family of priests with any of these false accusations.

22.9.0.en: The runners (guards): soldiers trained for swift movement, from whom came the royal guard that stood before Saul.

22.9.1.en: Despite Ahimelech's strong defense of himself and his truthfulness in all that he said, Saul's wrath and anger blinded him, as if he had heard nothing, and with injustice and tyranny in his opinion he pronounced the sentence of death on Ahimelech and all the priests, and asked his men standing with him to carry out his unjust sentence, justifying his sentence by the priests' conspiracy with David and their concealing the truth. But the men could not do this abominable deed and stain their hands with the blood of the priests of God Most High, who were honored by all the people, whom God commanded to be honored, who offered the sacrifices, interpreted the laws and led the people even in wars. It appears from this that the runners were more righteous than the king, respecting the priesthood and refusing injustice.

22.10.0.en: The ephod: white linen cloth that was among the priests' garments.

22.10.1.en: Saul noticed the disobedience of his special guard and their refusal to kill the priests, and this did not turn him from what his heart was stirred up with, so he looked to "Doeg the Edomite" and asked him to carry out the same order. This wicked man, who did not belong to the people of God at all but was of the offspring of "Esau", responded, and indeed he killed 85 priests wearing the linen ephod of the priests.

22.11.0.en: The matter went beyond every limit, for this wicked man also went to "Nob", the city of the priests and the present place of the tabernacle of meeting, and killed all the remaining priests with their wives and innocent children, and even the animals did not escape from this hideous massacre. Saul here, because he was a follower of Satan, ruins himself, because he ruins a city that belongs to him and not a city belonging to the enemies, just as the wicked person ruins his own senses and thoughts by himself instead of resisting Satan.

22.11.1.en: Anger is blind and leads a person to the worst sins. Examine yourself and do not make a decision in your anger, but flee from anger and control yourself and your nerves and ask God for calm, lest you commit a mistake that is hard to mend.

22.12.s.en: (4) The flight and escape of Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech

22.12.0.en: Abiathar the son of Ahimelech did not go with the priests to meet Saul, but remained at Nob inside the tabernacle to complete the service, and this was the reason for his escape and not being killed. After he saw all that had happened, he left "Nob" and fled to "David", who was also fleeing from the face of Saul, and when he found David he told him all the evil that Saul had done to the priests and how he had shed innocent blood.

22.13.0.en: David spoke with "Abiathar" the fugitive priest and told him that when he saw "Doeg the Edomite" at Nob, as he took the bread from his father Ahimelech, he expected that this wicked Edomite would be a troublemaker and would report to Saul what he had seen and add to it to kindle his wrath. David offered Abiathar an apology and expressed sorrow that he was the cause behind all these sad events, and this shows his humility.

22.14.0.en: David then asked Abiathar to stay with him, and of course this was what the man expected from David, and to reassure the man David gave him a covenant and a promise of protection, saying to him that whoever seeks to kill you seeks to kill me, the intended meaning being that David would never allow this. Thus there joined David the last priest remaining from Saul's dreadful crime, and Abiathar remained a priest with David all the days of his life. David's welcome of Abiathar shows his heart that was wide for all the persecuted, and God blessed him, as he alone came to have a priest who inquired of God. Through this evil that Saul did, God's word was fulfilled in the destruction of the house of Eli the priest because of his leniency with his two sons (ch. 2:31-36).

22.14.1.en: In proportion to Saul's evil was David's nobility of character, so he welcomed Abiathar to live with him and protected him. Be loving and helpful to others however wicked and selfish and abusive of others those around you may be, for you love people for the sake of God, who loved you and redeemed you and counts as great every love you offer to others and rewards you for it. David fights the Philistines, and Saul pursues David
